Estimate Hessian at a point based on sattered data

estimate_hessian.Rd

Estimate the Hessian at a given point x based on its neighboring scattered design points X and their evaluations y using locally-weighted polynomial regression (moving least squares).

Usage

estimate_hessian(x, X, y, bw = 1, kernel = "Epanech")

Arguments

x

A numeric vector of length D specifying the point at which to estimate Hessian.

X

A nXD (\(n \geq {D+2\choose 2}\)) matrix giving the locations of the neighboring points around x (It can contain x).

y

A numeric vector of length n giving the function evaluation at X.

bw

A positive real number giving the kernel bandwidth for locally weighted polynomial regression. Default to 1.

kernel

A character string specifying the type of kernel. Should be one of "Epanech" (Default), "RBF", "Tri-cube", "Triangular".

Value

A DxD matrix giving an estimate of the Hessian at x.

Details

The method performs a weighted least squares fit of a local quadratic polynomial centered at the point \(x\). The basis consists of all monomials of total degree up to 2: $$ \phi(z) = [1, z_1, \dots, z_d, z_1^2, z_1 z_2, \dots, z_d^2]^\top $$ where \(z_i = X_i - x_i\) is the centered design matrix.

Kernel weights are computed as: $$ w_i = K\left(\frac{\|X_i - x\|}{h}\right) $$ where \(K(\cdot)\) is the chosen kernel function. Supported kernels include:

- Epanechnikov (default): \(K(r) = \frac{3}{4}(1 - r^2)_+\)

- RBF: \(K(r) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} r^2\right)\)

- Tri-cube: \(K(r) = (1 - r^3)^3_+\)

- Triangular: \(K(r) = (1 - r)_+\)

The design matrix \(\Phi\) is built by evaluating all degree-0, 1, and 2 monomials at each centered design point.

The weighted normal equations are solved: $$ \hat{\beta} = (\Phi^\top W \Phi)^{-1} \Phi^\top W y $$ The estimated Hessian matrix is formed by applying second-order derivative operators \(D^\alpha\) to the basis at the origin: $$ H_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^N y_k \cdot a_k^{(\alpha)}, \quad \text{where } \alpha = e_i + e_j $$ and \(a^{(\alpha)} = W \Phi (\Phi^\top W \Phi)^{-1} D^\alpha \phi(0)\).

The function ensures that the output matrix \(H\) is symmetric by construction.

Examples

# (Not run)
set.seed(42)
f <- function(x) sin(x[1]) + cos(x[2]) + x[1]*x[2]
X <- matrix(runif(20, -0.1, 0.1), ncol = 2)
y <- apply(X, 1, f)
x0 <- c(0, 0)
H <- estimate_hessian(x0, X, y)
print(H)
#>             [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] -0.02069504  1.0027398
#> [2,]  1.00273978 -0.9945689
H_true <- numDeriv::hessian(f, x0)
print(H_true)
#>              [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] 9.436974e-07  0.9999996
#> [2,] 9.999996e-01 -1.0000001
